quick.summary: Why leaders skip your design documents, and how to fix your headers.
quick.takeaway: Make headings stand out, and write the full point instead of a vague label.

parts.title: Clear headings

beats.line: No one read my giant design proposal. How do I fix this?
Think of a highway. You do not read every sign you pass.
True. I only read the huge green exit signs.
Readers are driving fast too. They only look for the big signs.
We call this establishing a strong information hierarchy.
Can I just say clear headings? Hierarchy sounds like corporate speak.
Make them stand out so readers can scan the whole page quickly.
Making the font larger is easy. But what should they actually say?

parts.cliff: The best headings tell a story on their own.

beats.line: Do not write labels. Imagine if a newspaper just said, the weather.
I would not know if I needed an umbrella or a jacket.
Exactly. Your headings need to make a full point too.
Instead of writing, user research, write, users struggled to find the button.

board.text: users struggled to find the button

beats.line: Oh, I see. The heading gives the result of the section.
Yes. A busy director can read just the bold text.
And they still understand my entire argument without reading everything.
Now your document is a fast drive.
The new checkout flow is faster. That is my heading for the summary.

quiz.question: Which heading is the most effective for a fast reader skimming your document?
options: The results of the recent test
quiz.explanation: It tells the reader the actual result. The other options are just vague labels that force them to read the paragraph.

quiz.question: Good headings allow a busy reader to skim your document and still grasp your main argument.
quiz.explanation: If your headings make full points, a reader can skip the body text entirely and still understand the story.
